h1:
First Time in Phuket
What to Know + a 3-Day Plan
intro: If this is your first trip to Phuket, the good news is the island has it all in one place: the Andaman Sea, the Sino-Portuguese old town, punchy southern Thai food, and island-hopping trips you won't find anywhere else. But there are a few things that, if you know them ahead of time, make the whole trip go a lot smoother — from which month to come and when to dodge the monsoon to how to get from the airport into town without getting fleeced on the fare. We've gathered everything a friend who comes here often would quietly tell you, all in one place, and we close with an unrushed 3-day plan we've laid out for you.

blocks.html: Phuket is a bigger island than many people expect — driving from the far north to the far south takes the better part of an hour, and each zone has a completely different feel. The west coast is all long sandy beaches like Patong, Kata and Karon, while Phuket Town sits on the southeast side, an old quarter with Sino-Portuguese shophouses and great food. On a first visit there's no need to rush and tick off the whole island. Pick two or three modes you like and take it slow, then save the rest for next time.

blocks.text: The Most Important Thing — When to Go, Which Months to Skip the Monsoon

blocks.html: Phuket has two clear seasons, and picking the wrong window genuinely affects your trip — especially if you're coming to swim or island-hop. May through October is the southwest monsoon: the west-coast beaches (Patong, Kata, Karon, Surin) get strong surf and rip currents, this is the stretch when you hear about tourist drownings every year, and boat trips out to the islands can be cancelled if the sea is closed. November through April is the dry season — calm seas, clear skies, and the best time of all for swimming and island-hopping.

items: November–February (high season) — the best window for first-timers. Calm seas, good sun, little rain, island trips run every day. But it's peak season in full force: rooms fill up fast and prices hit their high, so book several months ahead.

March–April (late high season / hot) — the sea is still lovely and the water clear, but it's seriously hot. Crowds start to thin after Songkran and prices begin to drop, so this is a good-value stretch.

May–October (low season / monsoon) — rain comes in bursts rather than all day, rooms drop 50–70%, and you'll find stay-longer-get-a-free-night deals. But the west-coast surf is strong, so watch for red flags especially carefully.

August–September — the heaviest monsoon, with waves reaching 4–6 metres on some days. Better suited to the chill crowd who'd rather relax at the resort and eat and explore in town than get in the water.

blocks.title: A Red Flag Means No Swimming
blocks.html: Phuket's beaches use a flag system: green = safe, yellow = caution, red = absolutely no swimming. In the monsoon, Patong has the strongest rip currents on the island, and every year people die because they ignored a red flag and went in anyway. Don't take it lightly even if you're a strong swimmer — if you see a red flag, watch the sea from the sand instead.

blocks.text: Getting from the Airport into Town Without Overpaying

blocks.html: Phuket Airport (HKT) sits at the very north of the island, a fair way from Patong and the town (about 45 minutes to 1 hour depending on traffic). This catches a lot of first-timers off guard on the fare, because Phuket has no metered taxis like Bangkok does. Knowing your options ahead of time helps a lot.

items: Shared minibus (airport shuttle) — the cheapest, around 200 THB per person, from the public transport counter inside the airport. It runs roughly every 30 minutes and takes a while because it drops off at several stops (around 60–90 minutes to Patong).

Grab / Bolt — you see the price before you book, which makes it the easiest for first-timers. Around 600–900 THB into Patong or town depending on the time of day. Hail it from the pickup area the app points you to — the price is more certain and there's no haggling.
Airport taxi counter — a fixed flat fare of around 800 THB to Patong, booked at the counter in the terminal. Quick and no waiting, and it works out well for a group splitting the cost.
Hotel pickup — many resorts offer an airport transfer. Check the price when you book your room; sometimes it's included in the package or cheaper than arranging your own.

blocks.title: Watch Out for This
blocks.html: Don't take offers from people who approach you at the airport exit without checking the price, and don't get in any vehicle that won't tell you the fare clearly before you board. If you'd rather skip the headache, open Grab or Bolt and compare prices first — it's the safest reference point you have.

blocks.text: Getting Around the Island — Distances Are Bigger Than You Think

blocks.html: Phuket has no metro and no metered taxis, so there are only a few main ways to get around, and the thing that trips up first-timers is that "the distances between zones are bigger than you'd think." Patong to the old town, or out to Promthep Cape, takes about an hour. Planning your days one zone at a time saves you both time and money.

items: Grab / Bolt — convenient, and you see the price before booking, which makes it easiest for first-timers. But fares in Phuket run higher than in other cities and cars can be hard to find in some zones — in Patong in the evening you may wait a while, so build in extra time.

Tuk-tuks / local songthaews — a Phuket icon, but fares are fairly steep and there's no meter, so always agree on the price clearly before you get in. Even a short hop within Patong can run into the hundreds, so ask the price every single time.

Scooter rental — a Honda Click 125 runs around 150–300 THB/day, nimble and cheap if you can ride. Carry an international driving permit and wear a helmet — but Phuket's roads climb and drop steeply over the hills and traffic is fast, so don't push it if you're not used to riding.

Car rental — good if you're a group or travelling with kids; you can explore zone by zone freely. There's some parking at the beaches and in the old town, but in high season Patong gets jammed and parking is hard to find.

blocks.title: Plan by Zone
blocks.html: Because the distances are long, don't build a day around Patong in the morning, the old town at midday, and Promthep Cape in the afternoon — you'll lose more time on the road than you spend sightseeing. We'd suggest one day = one zone: a west-coast beach day, an old-town day, an island-hopping day. You'll get far more out of each.

blocks.text: Which Area to Stay In for a First Visit

items.name: Patong
items.blurb: The liveliest beach — restaurants, bars, shopping, water sports, and the nightlife on Bangla Road, all in one zone. Great for people who like buzz and energy; this is not the quiet option.

items.name: Kata–Karon
items.blurb: Lovely sandy beaches with clear water, a more relaxed vibe than Patong but still with everything you need. Restaurants and stays across a range of prices — good for families, couples, and first-timers who want balance.

items.name: Phuket Old Town
items.blurb: Not on the beach, but you get the Sino-Portuguese old-town atmosphere, cafés, pastel shophouses, the real southern food, and prices cheaper than the beach. Great for culture, eating, and photos.

blocks.html: On a first visit, if you're not sure, we'd suggest staying in Kata or Karon — you get a lovely beach and an atmosphere that isn't as hectic as Patong, but it's still easy to get around. If you're all about nightlife and shopping, pick Patong; if you're about food and culture, stay in the old town. And if you can split your time, staying in two zones (beach + town) for a few nights each makes for a nicely balanced trip.

blocks.html: Food is the reason a lot of people come back to Phuket — because it's not just seafood here, but punchy southern Thai food and Hokkien-Peranakan dishes you won't taste anywhere else. Many of the famous spots are in the old town. We've ordered them by how much we'd nudge a first-timer to try each one, with the names of places that are actually open right now.

items.name: Phuket Hokkien Mee
items.blurb: Yellow noodles stir-fried in dark soy with pork and seafood — a Phuket signature that's hard to find elsewhere, rich and smoky from the wok. It comes both dry-fried and in a soup; try it once and you'll understand why it's so well known.

items.name: Morning Dim Sum — Boonrat Dim Sum
items.blurb: A long-standing dim sum spot in town, with recipes handed down from Cantonese roots over the years. Locals here really do eat dim sum for breakfast — steamed buns, pork and shrimp and crab dumplings, dipped in local soy. Friendly prices, opens early, and packed.

items.name: Southern-Peranakan — Tu Kab Khao
items.blurb: Set in a 120-year-old shophouse in the old town, with a Michelin Bib Gourmand. Bold southern Thai and Peranakan cooking in a handsome heritage building. Busy in the evenings, so book ahead.

items.name: Homestyle Southern Food — One Chun
items.blurb: A southern Thai and Phuket restaurant in the old town, around the Thepkrasattri-Dibuk streets. Honest homestyle flavours, easy on the wallet, in a warm old-building setting — a good first meal of the trip when you want a taste of real Phuket.

items.name: O-Aew
items.blurb: Phuket's classic hot-weather dessert — a jelly made from banana seeds with red syrup and shaved ice, topped with red beans. The texture is chewy and cooling, and you'll find it around the old town. Cheap, and perfect after a walk through the market.

items.name: Fresh Seafood — Rawai / Beachfront Spots
items.blurb: You can't come to Phuket and not eat seafood. Pick it by the kilo at Rawai market and have a restaurant cook it, or hit a beachfront spot in Patong or Kata — lobster, crab, shellfish, mantis shrimp, all fresh. Choose places that state the price per kilo clearly before you order.

items.name: Tea & Roti (Muslim Breakfast)
items.blurb: Phuket's tea-and-roti culture is a big deal — roti fried crisp outside and soft inside, eaten with curry or condensed milk, paired with hot pulled tea. An easy-to-find breakfast or snack across the island, and cheap.

items.name: Sunday Walking Street Food (Lard Yai)
items.blurb: If your visit lands on a Sunday, Thalang Road in the old town turns into a walking street about 360 metres long, packed with street food savoury and sweet, local snacks, and regional finds. A lovely long graze, with no entry fee.

blocks.title: Seafood-Ordering Tip
blocks.html: When you order seafood by the kilo, always check the price per kilo and watch it weighed in front of you before it's cooked, so there's no surprise when the bill comes. And if you want fresh seafood at a good price, Rawai market in the morning has more to choose from and is cheaper than the touristy beachfront spots.

blocks.text: An Unrushed 3-Day Plan for a First Visit

blocks.html: This plan is laid out one zone per day so you don't waste time on the road — you'll get the beaches, the old town, and an island trip without running around all day. Adjust the timings to your style; every day has downtime built in. And try to line up the walking-street day with a Sunday so you don't miss it.

items.activity: Ease into the morning at Kata or Karon beach — swim or lie on the sand
items.note: In the dry season the sea is calm enough to swim; in the monsoon check the flag first — a red flag means absolutely no swimming.

items.activity: Lunch at a beachfront spot, then rest out of the sun through the early afternoon
items.note: The afternoon sun is strong; take shade or head back to your room for an hour.

items.activity: Head up to Karon Viewpoint (the Three Beaches viewpoint)
items.note: You'll see Kata Noi, Kata and Karon lined up beautifully — a classic Phuket photo spot.

items.activity: Go to Promthep Cape for sunset
items.note: The most famous sunset spot on the island. Get there early — it gets crowded and parking fills up fast.

items.activity: Seafood dinner around Rawai, or head back to your zone
items.note: Rawai is near Promthep Cape — pick seafood by the kilo and have it cooked fresh.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Phuket Old Town + Big Buddha + Wat Chalong

items.activity: Dim sum breakfast Phuket-style (e.g. Boonrat Dim Sum)
items.note: Dim sum is a popular breakfast for locals here; the famous spots get packed, so go a little early.

items.activity: Wander the old town — Thalang Road + Soi Romanee — and photograph the Sino-Portuguese shophouses
items.note: Lovely old pastel buildings; Soi Romanee has been ranked among the world's prettiest streets, lined with cafés and souvenir shops.

items.activity: Lunch on southern-Peranakan food in the old town (e.g. One Chun / Tu Kab Khao)
items.note: Popular spots get busy at midday; if you're going to the Michelin place, book ahead.

items.activity: Stop at Wat Chalong, Phuket's most important temple
items.note: Open roughly 07:00–17:00, no entry fee. Dress modestly — cover shoulders and knees.

items.activity: Head up to the Big Buddha for island views
items.note: In 2026 it's under restoration after a 2024 landslide; parts are still off-limits. You can reach the viewpoint/parking area — check the status before you go.

items.activity: If it's a Sunday, walk the Lard Yai walking street (Thalang Road)
items.note: Open Sunday 16:00–22:00, street food and local goods filling the road, no entry fee.

items.activity: Leave your accommodation and board an island-hopping boat tour (Phi Phi / Koh Maithon / Phang Nga Bay)
items.note: Tours include hotel transfers; book ahead and check the sea is open — in the monsoon they can be cancelled.

items.activity: Snorkel over the coral and fish / swim at the stops the tour takes you to
items.note: Listen to the guide about swim spots and the boat's return time; bring reef-safe sunscreen.

items.activity: Lunch on the island or on the boat (included in most tours)
items.note: Most tours include lunch and water; check the package details when you book.

items.activity: Back at the pier/hotel — rest up
items.note: Island-hopping is more tiring than you'd expect; leave time to rest before dinner.

items.activity: A farewell dinner + souvenir shopping in the old town
items.note: Phuket souvenirs like nam prik kung siap (shrimp paste chilli dip) and local snacks are cheaper in the old town than at the beach.

blocks.title: About Island-Hopping Tours
blocks.html: Book island tours with an operator that has real reviews and a clear licence. Check whether park fees are included (Phi Phi and Phang Nga Bay have separate national-park entry fees), and if you're going in the monsoon, confirm with the operator that the sea is open before you travel — on some days the Marine Department orders boats not to sail.

items: Respect the beach flags — a red flag means no swimming, not a suggestion. Rip currents in the monsoon are genuinely dangerous; always check the lifeguards and the flags before going in.
Agree the tuk-tuk/songthaew fare before you board — Phuket has no meters and fares run higher than you'd think, so settle the price clearly first, or use Grab/Bolt where the price is fixed.
Dress modestly at temples — Wat Chalong and others require covered shoulders and knees; some temples lend cover-ups, but bringing your own is easier.
Sunscreen and water — the Andaman sun is fierce, so wear sunscreen and carry water. If you're snorkelling, choose reef-safe sunscreen so you don't damage the coral.
Book accommodation and tours ahead — in high season (Nov–Feb) rooms in the popular areas fill fast and prices jump, and the well-known island tours sell out. Booking early pays off.
Carry some cash — markets, beachfront spots and songthaews are often cash-only, even though bigger places now take QR payments.

faq.q: When is the best time for a first trip to Phuket?
faq.a: The best window is November through February (high season) — calm seas, clear skies, little rain, swimming and island-hopping every day. But rooms fill fast and prices peak, so book ahead. May through October is the monsoon: rooms are much cheaper, but the west-coast surf is strong with rip currents, so watch for red flags especially carefully.

faq.q: How do you get from Phuket Airport into town, and how much does it cost?
faq.a: The cheapest is a shared minibus, around 200 THB per person, but it takes a while because it makes several stops. Grab/Bolt into Patong or town runs about 600–900 THB depending on the time of day, and you see the price before booking. The airport taxi counter has a fixed flat fare of around 800 THB to Patong. The airport is at the far north of the island, so allow roughly 45 minutes to 1 hour for the trip.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Phuket for a first visit, and where should you stay?
faq.a: For a first visit, 3 days is about right — you get the beaches, the old town, and one island-hopping day. For where to stay, if you're unsure go with Kata or Karon, since the beach is lovely and it's less hectic than Patong. If you're all about nightlife and shopping, pick Patong; if you're about food and culture, stay in the old town.

faq.q: Can you swim in Phuket during the monsoon?
faq.a: From May through October the west-coast beaches (Patong, Kata, Karon) get strong surf and rip currents, and there are tourist drownings reported every year. A red flag means absolutely no swimming, even if you're a strong swimmer. This stretch is better suited to relaxing at the resort, eating and exploring in town, and choosing land-based activities rather than getting into the open sea.

faq.q: Can you go up to the Big Buddha in Phuket in 2026?
faq.a: In 2026 the Big Buddha is under restoration after a 2024 landslide. Parts of the main area and close-up access to the statue are still closed; you can reach some of the viewpoint and parking areas. It's open roughly 06:00–19:00. We'd suggest checking the latest status before you go, as the restoration plan may change.
